A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same memorization study. Their text, definitions, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching v1 Appendices F–H to v2 Appendices H–J.

before.justification: V1 reports original memorization measurements across RLHF stages, KL-penalty and learning-rate experiments, and benchmark evaluations of its trained models.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds IPO experiments and memorization evaluations across additional datasets, domains, and model scales.

M1.justification: The original RLHF procedure and counterfactual-memorization measurement method remain unchanged. IPO is an existing alternative added to the empirical comparison; the paper does not introduce a new algorithmic component or modify its original measurement procedure.

E1.justification: Section 5.5 and Appendix G add CodeXGLUE CodeCompletion-line and extend memorization analysis beyond code to natural-language data: Anthropic HH for reward modeling and LIMA for RL fine-tuning. The original SD, PD, and HumanEval coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Section 5.4 adds an evaluated direct-preference alternative, IPO on Gemma 2B and 7B, to the RLHF and supervised-fine-tuning comparisons. DPO is discussed but not evaluated. Table 2 retains CodeGemma 2B, DeepSeek Coder 2B, and StarCoder2 3B.

E3.justification: Added experiments use Gemma 2B/7B with their pretrained controls, and larger RLHF configurations with Gemini Nano reward models, Gemini Pro policies, and a base Gemini Pro control. Figure 8 specifies separate CodeXGLUE splits and subsampling CodeXGLUE and Anthropic HH to SD.Base's size. These are additional protocols; the original experiments' stated settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 5.5 and Figures 7–8 newly test whether low memorization depends on synthetic code, task domain, or reward/policy model scale. Section 5.4 also examines IPO memorization at two scales. The original KL, learning-rate, reward-label ablations, and memorized examples are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-training-run counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty estimates for the memorization results. The existing description of different random seeds for synthetic-example generation is retained.

E6.justification: Original results, including 17.6% fine-tuning versus 0.9% RLFT memorization on SD.Base and Table 2's scores, are retained. V2 adds IPO rates of 18.2% and 19.5% on SD.Base for Gemma 2B and 7B, respectively, and 0.6% on SD.Links for both. Figures 7–8 add results across scales and datasets. These are additional experimental conditions, not same-setting performance improvements.

T1.justification: Definition 3.1, approximate counterfactual memorization, and the sliding-window reasoning are unchanged. The added discussion of DPO and IPO provides conceptual background without introducing formal definitions, derivations, theorems, or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract and contributions add claims that IPO memorizes preference data more readily than RLHF and that the findings hold across datasets, tasks, and model scales. V2 explicitly presents RLHF as safer for sensitive preference data, expanding v1's contribution beyond analysis of the three RLHF stages.

C2.justification: V1 leaves direct preference learning and larger-model behavior as future questions. V2 interprets its new evidence as showing that low reward-data leakage is not specific to synthetic code or small models, and cautions against direct preference learning despite its simplicity. Existing qualifications about sensitive-data identification and code-related confounders remain.

D1.justification: V2 supplies limited setup details for the added experiments, particularly Figure 8's dataset pairings, separate splits, and size matching. Original hardware, hyperparameter, provenance, and synthetic-data construction information is retained. Detailed training recipes for the new IPO and scaling experiments are not supplied.

R1.justification: Direct preference learning becomes central to the paper's positioning, whereas v1 mentions DPO mainly as future work. Section 2.1 adds the DPO–PsiPO distinction and motivates selecting IPO through Azar et al. V2 also substantially expands citations to memorization/privacy research and the newly evaluated datasets.

P1.justification: V2 expands the abstract, introduction, and Section 2.1, adds Sections 5.4–5.5 and Appendices F–G, and revises the discussion. Most existing prose and the main section order remain intact; old Appendices F–H become H–J. The changes chiefly integrate new scientific content rather than extensively rewrite the document.

P2.justification: V2 adds Figures 6–8: IPO scatterplots, a model/dataset comparison bar chart, and three reward-data memorization panels. Existing plots are retained, with the original Figure 6 becoming Figure 9. Figure 4 is reduced and wrapped beside text, several displays are resized, and Tables 1–2 are brought together without changing their contents.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's dependence on one small policy model and synthetic code through larger-model, additional-code, and natural-language evaluations in Section 5.5 and Appendix G. It also investigates direct preference learning, explicitly left for future work in v1. These additions strengthen the empirical basis and applicability of the central findings. The broad recommendation favoring RLHF remains less secure because IPO and RLHF use different backbones and controls, and the added experiments lack detailed training recipes and uncertainty estimates. Those limitations temper the interpretation but do not outweigh the substantial validation gains.
